result: A comprehensive MET kinase domain variant library was constructed spanning amino acids 1059-1345, synthesized by Twist Bioscience with one mammalian high-usage codon per amino acid, containing >99% of all possible 5764 kinase domain mutations. The library includes fill-in controls and mutations at positions with failed synthesis, introduced into two cloning backbones (wild-type and exon 14 skipped).
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C101-C103 provide detailed methodological description of library construction with explicit statements about coverage, synthesis, and design. The >99% coverage claim is supported by citation to prior work (Estevam et al., 2024) and methodological details are clearly described.

result: Ba/F3 cells were used as a selection system due to undetectable endogenous RTK expression and IL-3 addiction. TPR-MET fusion generates IL-3-independent constitutive activity, creating a sensitive system for detecting growth reduction from small molecule inhibition, though membrane-proximal effects are lost.
evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C83-C85, C96-C97 describe the experimental system with citation support and explicit quality control measures (IL-3 dependence checks, cell density maintenance). The characterization of system advantages and limitations is appropriately documented.

result: Eleven inhibitors were selected for screening: six type I inhibitors (crizotinib, capmatinib, tepotinib, glumetinib, savolitinib, NVP-BVU972), three type II inhibitors (cabozantinib, glesatinib analog, merestinib), and one proposed type III inhibitor (tivantinib). Four of these (crizotinib, cabozantinib, tepotinib, capmatinib) are FDA-approved for MET.
evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C86-C88 explicitly state the inhibitor panel composition with citation support for FDA approval status. The selection is clearly documented in methods and results sections.

result: Deep mutational scanning was performed with time points selected every two cell doublings over four time points, cells maintained at IC50 for each inhibitor without IL-3. All samples were processed in parallel and sequenced on the same Illumina NovaSeq 6000 flow cell. Variant fitness scores were calculated using Rosace with normalization to reflect cell doubling rates.
evaluation: Claims C71-C74, C78, C110-C122 provide comprehensive methodological details for the DMS experiment. The parallel processing and same-flowcell sequencing (C73, C122) are important controls for batch effects. The Rosace normalization approach (C74, C78) is explicitly described and cited.

result: Tivantinib displayed equivalent inhibition regardless of IL-3 presence (r=0.93 correlation with DMSO), demonstrating MET-independent cytotoxicity, in contrast to crizotinib which only showed inhibitory effects under IL-3 withdrawal. This contradicts tivantinib's proposed type III MET-selective mechanism despite in vitro evidence of catalytic activity inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C16-C19, C79-C82 present a clear experimental test (Figure 2E) distinguishing MET-dependent from MET-independent effects. The high correlation with DMSO (C19) and IL-3-independent inhibition (C16) provide strong evidence for off-target effects, supported by citations to contradictory prior literature (C80-C82).

result: Inhibitor correlation analysis revealed that capmatinib showed the greatest difference from DMSO (r=0.45), type II inhibitors displayed the greatest similarities to one another (merestinib and glesatinib analog r=0.93), and AMG-458 (type I½) displayed higher similarity to type II than type I inhibitors, likely due to R-spine interactions.
evaluation: Claims C20-C22, C61-C62 present correlation data (Figure 2B-C) with explicit Pearson correlation values. The structural rationalization for AMG-458 similarity to type II inhibitors (C61) is supported by reference to binding mode (Figure 1B).

result: DMSO control populations displayed a bimodal distribution centered around 0, while inhibitor-treated populations showed distributions with loss-of-function peaks and right-skewed distributions with greater enrichment of gain-of-function scores at positive tails.
evaluation: Claims C75-C77 describe the fitness score distributions (Figure 2A) with explicit characterization of expected patterns. The bimodal DMSO distribution and right-skewed inhibitor distributions are clearly shown in the data.

result: G1163 and D1228 are positions with the highest frequency of resistance mutations across all inhibitor types. G1163 is at the solvent front entrance and D1228 stabilizes an inactive A-loop conformation. M1211, a C-spine residue, also showed resistance across inhibitors. Specific mutations at these sites (D1228N/H/V/Y, Y1230C/H/N/S, G1163R) have been noted in prior clinical reports. Across all inhibitor types, 17 shared variants were identified.
evaluation: Claims C23-C26, C34, C56-C57 identify common resistance hotspots with structural rationalization (C24-C25) and literature support (C57). The data is presented in Figure 6A-D with explicit frequency counts. The structural explanations are consistent with known inhibitor binding modes.

result: Y1230 was a hotspot for type I and I½ inhibitors but not type II inhibitors, rationalized by Y1230's role in pi-stacking interactions with type I inhibitors. Conversely, F1200 and L1195 are hotspots for type II but not type I inhibitors, as both residues make direct contact with type II but not type I inhibitors.
evaluation: Claims C27-C29 demonstrate inhibitor-type-specific resistance patterns (Figure 6A-D) with structural rationalization. The differential resistance profiles are consistent with known binding modes and supported by citations (C28).

result: I1084 is enriched as a resistance site for type I inhibitors and is located at the solvent front of the P-loop. L1142 (R-spine residue) and L1140 (back of ATP-binding pocket) are enriched for type II inhibitor resistance, consistent with their spatial locations.
evaluation: Claims C30-C33 identify position-specific resistance patterns with structural rationalization and citation support (C30). The spatial logic connecting residue location to inhibitor type is sound and supported by structural data (Figure 6E-F).

result: Cabozantinib maintained the lowest average correlation with all type I inhibitors, making it the most divergent type II inhibitor. 44 mutations showed crizotinib resistance with cabozantinib sensitivity, and 3 showed the opposite profile. Y1093K showed a nearly 10-fold shift in crizotinib sensitivity with no difference in cabozantinib sensitivity, while L1195M was refractory to cabozantinib but sensitive to crizotinib.
evaluation: Claims C35-C39 present differential sensitivity analysis (Figure 7) with statistical filtering and experimental validation via dose-response curves (Figure 7D). The identification of non-cross-resistant mutations is supported by both DMS data and orthogonal validation experiments.

result: Previously discovered mutations are strongly shifted to a GOF distribution for drugs where resistance is reported, while distributions are centered around neutral for other drugs. H1094Y demonstrated slight sensitivity to glesatinib in the assay, suggesting resistance may be linked to exon14 deletion, L1195V mutation, or cellular factors not modeled by Ba/F3.
evaluation: Claims C59-C60 validate the DMS approach against literature (Figure 4C) and identify a discrepancy (C60) with appropriate caveats about system limitations. The validation strengthens confidence in novel findings while acknowledging uncertainty.

result: ESM-1b predicts fitness in DMSO (r=0.50) better than inhibitor-treated datasets (r=0.28), likely because inhibitor fitness doesn't reflect evolutionary pressures. An augmented XGBoost model incorporating biophysical and chemical features improved performance from 0.28 to 0.37 correlation. Monotonic constraints were used to prevent overfitting, and Umol was used to predict variant-inhibitor structures.
evaluation: Claims C40-C41, C89-C94 present machine learning analysis with clear baseline performance (C40), improvement metrics (C41), and methodological details (C92-C94). The modest improvement (0.28 to 0.37) is honestly reported. The rationale for ESM-1b's limitation (C91) is reasonable. However, the improvement is relatively small and the model's predictive power remains limited.

result: Y1093 is located in β2 at the roof of the ATP-binding site and does not directly engage with crizotinib. Y1093 mutations may negatively impact crizotinib stability compared to ATP, potentially by perturbing β1-β2 packing. I1084 is in β1 at the roof of the ATP-binding pocket, and I1084H clashes with crizotinib's hinge-binding and solvent-front moieties without interfering with ATP.
evaluation: Claims C63-C66, C69-C70 identify resistance mutations with structural analysis. However, the mechanisms are speculative (C64, C70 explicitly use 'speculate'). While the structural observations are sound (C65-C66), the mechanistic explanations lack experimental validation beyond the DMS data.

result: L1195 is an αE-helix position with previously recorded resistance (L1195V/F), confirmed as a type II-only resistance hotspot. Mutations like Met or Phe at position 1195 clash with cabozantinib's fluorophenyl moiety used to access the back pocket, unlike crizotinib which occupies the solvent front.
evaluation: Claims C67-C68 identify L1195 as a type II-specific resistance site with structural rationalization and literature support. The mechanism is consistent with known type II binding modes and validated by dose-response data (C39, Figure 7D).

result: Small-molecule kinase inhibitors fall into four groups based on ATP pocket binding and conformational preferences. Type I inhibitors occupy the adenosine pocket and form hinge hydrogen bonds. Type II inhibitors extend into the R-spine opening. Type I½ inhibitors combine features of both. Type III inhibitors are allosteric. Type I MET inhibitors leverage Y1230 pi-stacking and D1228-K1110 salt-bridge. Tepotinib and capmatinib are classified as type Ia based on G1163 solvent-front interaction.
evaluation: Claims C9-C15, C53-C54 describe inhibitor classification with citation support and structural analysis. The reclassification of tepotinib and capmatinib as type Ia (C14-C15) is based on structural analysis (Figure 1) and explicitly acknowledges disagreement with other studies, which is appropriate scientific practice.

result: MET is an RTK and proto-oncogene implicated in multiple cancers. Clinical reports document recurrent resistance mutations at D1228, Y1230, G1163, L1195. The juxtamembrane domain (exon 14) serves a negative regulatory function and is recurrently excluded in cancer. RTK disruption through mutations, amplification, fusions, or autocrine loops drives cancer. TKIs like imatinib show durable outcomes, but resistance emerges through mutations affecting kinase stability, expression, conformation, or activity. Sequential treatment of type I and II inhibitors is a general approach to combating resistance.
evaluation: Claims C42-C52, C55 provide background context with appropriate citations. These are established facts from the literature and provide necessary context for the study. All claims are properly cited.

result: Methodological details for computational and experimental procedures are provided, including: inhibitors lacking structures were docked using AutoDock Vina; inhibitors were purchased from SelleckChem; dose-response curves were fitted with GraphPad Prism; libraries were transformed in MegaX cells and propagated to OD 0.5; library coverage was determined by colony counts; viral packaging used Lipofectamine3000 in Plat-E cells; spinfection at MOI 0.1 in triplicate; puromycin selection; sequencing files were demultiplexed; reads were filtered with BBDuk and mapped with BBMap; variants were analyzed with GATK and filtered by count thresholds; normalized counts were regressed on time intervals.
evaluation: Claims C95, C99-C100, C104-C109, C123-C127 provide detailed methodological information that is standard for the field. The methods are clearly described with appropriate tool citations and parameter specifications, enabling reproducibility.

result: Plat-E cells stably expressing retroviral envelope and packaging plasmids were originally gifted by Dr. Wendell Lim.
evaluation: Claim C98 provides appropriate attribution for a reagent. This is standard practice and properly documented.
